title: Design Tic-Tac-Toe
summary: An n×n board where every move must report a winner in O(1). The board is a decoy — you never need it. The interview turns on whether you spot that a win is four running counters, not a scan.

blocks.title: What you are actually being asked
blocks.text: Two different questions hide behind one title. The **coding** version (LeetCode 348) wants `move()` in O(1) and the board is a red herring. The **design** version wants classes, an extensible win rule and a playable game. Ask which one you are in — the answers barely overlap, and guessing wrong burns twenty minutes.

Implement `TicTacToe(int n)` with one method: `int move(int row, int col, int player)`, returning the winning player or `0`. Moves are guaranteed valid and non-repeating. A player wins by filling any row, column, or either diagonal.
The naive answer, and why it is not enough
Keep an `n × n` grid; after each move, check that row, that column and both diagonals. Correct, easy, **O(n) per move** — and the stated follow-up asks you to beat it.

blocks.title: You never need the board
blocks.text: A win means *n marks of one player in a line*. You do not need to know **which** cells — only **how many**. So keep a counter per line, add +1 for player 1 and −1 for player 2, and a line is won the moment its counter hits ±n. The grid disappears entirely.

blocks.title: Four families of counters
blocks.caption: `rows[i]`, `cols[j]`, and two scalars for the diagonals. A move touches at most four of them, so `move` is O(1) time and the whole game is O(n) space instead of O(n²).
blocks.code:
graph TD M["move(r, c, player)
delta = +1 or −1"] M --> R["rows[r] += delta"] M --> C["cols[c] += delta"] M --> D{"r == c ?"} D -- yes --> DG["diag += delta"] M --> AD{"r + c == n−1 ?"} AD -- yes --> AG["anti += delta"] R --> W{"|counter| == n ?"} C --> W DG --> W AG --> W W -- yes --> WIN[["return player"]] W -- no --> NO[["return 0"]] classDef win fill:#153229,stroke:#34d399,color:#f2f2f7 class WIN win

blocks.title: The centre cell on an odd board
blocks.text: On a 3×3, cell (1,1) is on **both** diagonals. Two separate `if`s — not `if / else if` — is the whole fix, and using `else if` is the most common bug in submitted solutions. It passes small tests and fails the diagonal case.

blocks.title: What the counter trick gives up
blocks.text: You can no longer print the board, undo a move, or answer *“is this cell taken?”* — you threw that information away. If the interviewer wants a **playable** game, keep the grid **and** the counters: O(n²) space, still O(1) moves. Volunteering that trade is worth more than the trick itself.
If the interviewer wants classes rather than counters, the shape changes completely — and the extension point is the win rule, because that is what the follow-ups will move.

blocks.title: When they want an object model
blocks.caption: `WinRule` behind an interface is what makes “now make it connect-4” a new class rather than a rewrite.
blocks.code:
classDiagram
    class Game {
        -Board board
        -List~Player~ players
        -int currentTurn
        -WinRule rule
        +MoveResult play(int row, int col)
    }
    class Board {
        -Mark[][] cells
        +boolean isEmpty(int r, int c)
        +void place(int r, int c, Mark m)
        +boolean isFull()
    }
    class WinRule {
        <<interface>>
        +boolean isWin(Board b, int r, int c, Mark m)
    }
    WinRule <|.. NInARowRule
    WinRule <|.. KInARowRule
    Game o-- Board
    Game --> WinRule

items.title: n×m board with k-in-a-row
items.text: Reported verbatim at Databricks. The counter trick **dies here** — a run of k can start anywhere, so counters no longer identify a line. Scan outward from the placed cell in four directions, counting both ways: O(k) per move, which is still far better than O(n·m).

items.title: Detect a draw
items.text: Count moves. On an n×n board a draw is `moves == n*n` with no winner — O(1), and it is the follow-up people forget.

items.title: Support undo
items.text: Now you need the board and a move stack. Counters are trivially reversible — subtract the delta — which is a nice property to point out.

items.title: More than two players
items.text: The ±1 trick only works for two. Generalise to a count per (line, player), which is O(n · p) space. Say why the trick was two-player-specific rather than pretending it generalises.

items.title: Play on an infinite board (Gomoku)
items.text: The board becomes a hash map of occupied cells and the win check is the k-in-a-row scan. This is the version that actually shows up in senior loops.

items.title: Add an AI opponent
items.text: Minimax with alpha-beta on 3×3 is exhaustive and instant; on larger boards it needs a heuristic and a depth limit.

blocks.text: Edge cases to state before you are asked

items: `n = 1` — one cell, and the first move wins on the row, the column and both diagonals at once.
The centre of an odd board sits on both diagonals; two independent `if`s, never `else if`.
The problem guarantees valid moves — say that you are trusting the contract rather than silently assuming it. If it did not, `move` needs an occupancy check, which means keeping the board.
A win is reported on the move that causes it, not on a later query.
Player values other than 1 and 2 break the ±1 encoding — validate or document.

rows: Asks whether this is the coding or the design version
Realises only *counts* matter, drops the board
Two separate checks, and explains the centre cell
Names what the counters give up
Recognises the trick does not survive it

blocks.title: The 45-minute plan
blocks.text: **0–4** ask which version. **4–8** state the naive O(n) scan and why the follow-up rules it out. **8–12** the counter insight, on the board, before any code. **12–22** write it — it is twenty lines. **22–30** edge cases: n=1, the centre cell, draws. **30–45** k-in-a-row, and be honest that it needs a different algorithm.
